summary: Describes an experiment in automated resource sharing between unlike systems. A user of the MUDDLE system at MIT-DMS could make use of the MACSYMA algebra system at MIT-Mathlab without knowing anything about the network or MACSYMA.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 578 describes a program that let MUDDLE users request mathematical work from MACSYMA on another computer. The program handled the Telnet connection and notation changes, though the authors note that this approach was less reliable than a purpose-built protocol would be.

questions: how did muddle use remote macsyma
how were muddle and macsyma expressions translated
subtitle: An experiment that let MUDDLE users call remote MACSYMA functions.

tldr.problem: Using MACSYMA from MUDDLE would otherwise require users to manage a remote connection and translate input and results themselves.
tldr.mechanism: Programs in MUDDLE connected to MACSYMA through Telnet, translated between MUDDLE prefix and MACSYMA infix notation, sent requests and interpreted the replies.
tldr.outcome: The experiment let MUDDLE users invoke selected MACSYMA operations through local functions, but the authors say a purpose-built resource-sharing protocol would be more reliable and efficient.

today: RFC 578 documents an experiment in automated access to a remote mathematical system over the ARPANET.

sections.title: A Remote Mathematical Resource
sections.content: The experiment connected MUDDLE at MIT-DMS to the MACSYMA system at MIT-Mathlab. Its goal was to let a MUDDLE user request a computation without needing to know about the ARPANET, Mathlab or MACSYMA. Unlike an earlier experiment described in the RFC, the user did not manually connect, log in, enter a request and retrieve a result.
sections.plainLanguage: A user could request a mathematical operation from MUDDLE without managing the connection to the other computer. Programs handled the remote work and returned the result to MUDDLE.

sections.title: Translating Requests and Results
sections.content:
The MUDDLE programs connected to the Mathlab logger service through Telnet, logged in and invoked MACSYMA. They converted MUDDLE's prefix-form expression into MACSYMA's infix form, sent the request, interpreted MACSYMA's output and converted a result back to MUDDLE form. The user could then use the returned result in other MUDDLE computations.

The RFC gives examples including integration, differentiation, expansion and simplification. It says the system recognized errors, but its interpretation of the terminal-oriented output was not foolproof.
sections.plainLanguage: MUDDLE translated an expression into MACSYMA's notation and sent it over Telnet. It then translated the answer back so the user could continue working in MUDDLE.

sections.title: Limits of the Experiment
sections.content:
The experiment used an interactive Telnet connection because the Mathlab site did not provide a MACSYMA server and no general resource-sharing protocol was available for this use. The authors explicitly say they are not recommending this as the general approach: a protocol designed for programs to use remote resources would be more reliable and efficient.

The program could mistake messages or other console activity for computation output. Users could switch to a verbose mode to inspect the interaction or enter direct communication with MACSYMA.
sections.plainLanguage: The system read output from a service designed for people at a terminal, so it could misread messages as answers. The authors say a protocol designed for automated resource sharing would work better.
